\chapter{O --- One Letter, One Catch}
\label{ch:o}
\hlchaptermodality{233}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can offer a choice between two things.}

I can offer a choice between two things.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[o]{o — one letter, one catch}

\label{lesson:ES-C61-o}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Y} joins two things: \emph{café} \emph{\textbf{y}} \emph{agua}.

Now the other one — not both, but a choice between them.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Café} \emph{\textbf{o}} \emph{agua?} — Coffee or water?
\end{quote}

\textbf{o} is the whole word. Latin's was \emph{\textbf{aut}}, and it wore all the way down to a single letter — which is about as far as a word can go without disappearing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
And that is the problem. A word one letter long is easy to lose.

Say \emph{siete o ocho} — \emph{seven or eight} — quickly, and the \emph{o} is swallowed by the \emph{o} of \emph{ocho}. So Spanish swaps it for a shape that cannot be swallowed:

\begin{quote}
\emph{siete} \emph{\textbf{u}} \emph{ocho}
\end{quote}

Nothing here is about meaning. \emph{O} becomes \emph{\textbf{u}} in front of a word that \textbf{begins with the \emph{o} sound} — including one spelled with a silent \emph{h}, because the \emph{h} is not there to be heard.

It is the same instinct you have now seen three times: \emph{mucho} into \emph{muy}, \emph{a el} into \emph{al}, and now \emph{o} into \emph{u}. Spanish keeps rearranging small words so the next one stays audible.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿Café o agua?}
  \item \emph{siete u ocho}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does \emph{o} become \emph{u}? (Before a word that \textbf{starts with the \emph{o} sound}.)

And is a silent \emph{h} an obstacle? (\textbf{No} — the rule listens, it does not read.)
\end{tcolorbox}
